P1.evidence: The application was read back with a specific and it landed — 'Yeah, I see the application that you're a semi-retired police officer' — which opened thirty-two years of service and set a warm tone. The open question was clean: 'brief me in. What's going on? What brought you here on this lovely day?' But there was no frame at all. Not a two-part or three-part version, none — the rep went from hello straight to discovery. Consequently there was no frame agreement either. On a call that ended in a hard money objection, the absence of any 'what you need' element in the open is not cosmetic: nothing early on established that a decision would be asked for or that an investment would be discussed.

P2.evidence: Six clean hits, and the sleep question earned its keep — 'how do you sleep?' produced the prostate and nocturia disclosure that nothing else would have surfaced. Age was asked directly, retirement and current activity were explored properly, and the nutrition sequence was the rep's usual strong work including the processed-food and guilty-pleasure probes. The injuries question was asked in the correct form: 'what kind of injuries, are there any, anything that's limiting your movements?'. Score it a hit for asking, but the evidence has to record what happened next: the prospect said 'No, surprisingly not' and then described two back surgeries, an L3-L4-L5 fusion, an unrecovered triceps tear with a specialist appointment the next day, and prior surgery after which he was told his lifting days were over — and the rep asked not one follow-up question about any of it. P2c is a clean miss; conditions were never asked, and the prostate issue and declining testosterone both arrived unprompted.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals phase in the batch. The bridge was asked twice and pushed past the easy answer — 'let me ask you this, like, why? Why all the struggle?' and then 'That's why I'm asking, what's your why? What's behind that? Apart from looking good.' The forward projection ran — 'six months down the line, what becomes possible for you?' — and when the prospect answered thinly with 'self-confidence, self-esteem, I guess', the rep challenged it rather than accepting it: 'You said confidence, like, you seem like a pretty confident guy, like, are you lacking confidence?'. P3f and P3g both ran properly: 'You mentioned you have a son?', 'Any grandkids?', 'Are you still, like, being active with him?', and then the identity frame 'you're the kind of dad that you still respect because you can kick your son's easily'. The reflect-back was a genuine reframe that moved the prospect off his own surface answer — 'you said you're a pretty vain person, it's hard for me to believe that... but the longevity part'. Only the two menu-style checks were skipped.

P4.evidence: Almost nothing was run. The bootcamp history and the enforced switch away from barbells after the ulnar nerve surgery both came out, but from the prospect's own narration; the rep's only related question was 'when you were on duty, you were very active throughout the day. Right?'. The prospect then handed over the entire root cause unprompted — 'a lot of times I find myself, I want a program. I want something to follow, a structured program. And I want to be accountable... I'm all over the place recently. And I want more structure. I want results. And I want guidance' — and no follow-up was asked. Why he has been unable to hold structure on his own, despite being a certified trainer who ran bootcamps for a police department, is the single most interesting question available on this call and it was never put to him.

P5.evidence: Absent again, and this is the fifth consecutive sales call in the batch with no consequence frame. The omission is starkest here because the prospect supplied the material himself, in detail and with feeling: a father who retired at 60, 'just wanted to be old', let himself go, and spent the last ten years of his life in a wheelchair before dying at 82, plus a younger brother who has lost his teeth and looks a decade older. The rep's response was to redirect to a positive future — 'you're going to be 70, you're going to be 80, and you're going to still be active'. Not one of the four scripted moves was used. Twenty minutes later a fixed-income buyer had to weigh $6,000 against nothing at all.

P6.evidence: Both checks ran, before the price, and the rep handled a soft answer well. On belief: 'do you feel that having this right training, the simple nutrition and accountability from Trevor built around you would actually get you to your goals?' produced 'I hope so', and rather than banking it the rep pushed — 'You hope so?' and then 'Why would it work for you?' — which made the prospect correct himself: 'I guess I used the wrong words. It should work for me... as long as I'm committed to it and I'm held accountable, and I have a guided program to follow.' The all-in check followed in the scripted form with a confirmation push: 'are you fully committed to actually showing up and doing the work?' / 'Oh, absolutely.' / 'You sure?'. P6c is partial because when the real hesitation arrived at the price, the script's instruction to return to Phase 5 was unavailable — there was no Phase 5 to return to.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and refused four times; payment and everything downstream were unreachable. N/A rather than miss. Note also that the recording terminates during a connection failure with no closing exchange, so even if anything further occurred it is not on tape.

objection_plays.detail: Ran further than on any other call in this batch and still stopped short. Isolation was clean and confirmed twice — 'let's put the finances aside for a second. Apart from the finances, is there anything else that would be keeping you from being fully committed?' and 'You sure? Nothing else? Keeping you from being 100% in?' / 'No, that's it. It's all about the money.' The upfront-versus-break-it-up move ran: 'most of the clients take it upfront. For certain clients, I don't feel that this is the best thing for their situation, so we can break it up.' The permission question ran too, which is rare in this corpus: 'are you comfortable in having such a conversation?' The financial picture then collapsed. Only the first item was attempted — 'what free cash on hand do you have, like maybe, savings, checkings account that you're able to dispose right now?' — and it was refused. Monthly surplus after bills, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available and investments were never asked. The 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' frame was not used. Critically, the rep inverted the sequence the script implies: he made the disclosure of payment options conditional on the prospect first disclosing his finances — 'I cannot tell you what the option would be for you if I don't know what you're capable of actually putting down' — which is what turned an exploration into an interrogation.

'That's something I'd have to sleep on, and I know you want a decision today' is a textbook trigger and the rep answered it with a one-liner: 'You want to sleep on it? Come on. It's not a pillow.' None of the seven scripted moves ran. He never asked whether the prospect felt this CAN get him to his goal, never asked what makes him feel it can, never asked what is actually preventing him from starting, never used 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and never used the man-you-want-to-be frame — which would have landed unusually well on a prospect who had just described his father's decline and his own determination not to repeat it.

The timing trigger fired twice and in substance: 'Maybe it's just not the right time for me' and 'Not at this time. It's just bad time... I got a couple of things I'm paying on now that will be paid up in a matter of months, and then I would be able to.' The rep ran nothing. He did not use 'things never slow down', did not ask when it actually becomes the right time, did not use the compounding argument about metabolism and injuries — which for a 62-year-old is the strongest version of that line available anywhere in this corpus — and did not offer 'what if all you had to do was show up'. He also failed to do the obvious commercial thing, which was to hear 'paid up in a matter of months' as a start date and book it.

Script gap, clinical: the prospect disclosed an L3-L4-L5 spinal fusion, a triceps tear under active specialist investigation with an appointment the following day, and explicit prior clinical advice that 'your lifting days are over'. There is no scripted screen, no clearance question and no disqualification path. The rep asked one question — 'anything that's limiting your movements?' — accepted 'No, surprisingly not', and proceeded to sell loaded ballistic kettlebell training. The playbook offers him nothing here.

Script gap, age-related efficacy doubt: 'part of me is, I am older, you know, but I can adapt.' There is no play for a prospect who doubts the programme will work on a 62-year-old body. The rep handled it obliquely and reasonably well through the 'Why would it work for you?' challenge, which prompted the prospect to talk himself back into it, but nothing about that was scripted and nothing addressed the underlying doubt directly.

Script gap, price expectation mismatch: 'I was expecting like 1,200, maybe 2,400, not 6 grand.' That is a 2.5x to 5x gap set before the call by whatever marketing brought him in, and there is no play for closing it. The rep did not acknowledge the gap, did not ask where the expectation came from, and did not mention that a product exists at roughly that price.

notes: Two things are true about this call and they need to be held separately. On the scored process it is one of the better calls in the batch — baseline and goals were both run properly, the reflect-back genuinely moved the prospect, and both commitment checks ran before the price with the rep correctly refusing to accept 'I hope so' as an answer. The Objection C play also ran further here than anywhere else in the corpus, including the permission question that everyone else skips. On conduct it is the worst call in the batch, and the adherence score should not be allowed to obscure that. The prospect declined four times and the selling continued past every one of them, including after he refused on privacy grounds to disclose his savings. Three coaching points, in order of importance. First: a fourth explicit decline from a 62-year-old on a fixed income is not an objection to be handled, and 'Do you want me to give up on you that easily' is not a play in this playbook or any other. Second: he told you the money frees up in months — that is a booked follow-up, not a loss. Third, and this is the pattern across the whole batch: he handed you his father in a wheelchair for ten years and his brother who looks a decade older, and you answered with an optimistic future-pace. Phase 5 exists precisely for that material, and skipping it is why the price had nothing to push against.
